{"id": "2:186/q10", "question": "What makes a person's call genuine and eligible for response?", "turns_on": "The sources give different analyses, reports, or applications of this wording.", "positions": [{"id": "2:186/q10/p1", "position": "Manners include praise, blessings, humility, good wording, and appropriate time or place.", "reasons": "THALABI, d. 427 (بعضهم): Prayer has manners and conditions that occasion an answer; whoever observes them qualifies for a response. MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 (author): One view says response is obligatory when conditions are complete because supplication is worship whose reward is an answer. MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 (author): When the supplicant falls short of the conditions, an answer is not obligatory. MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 (author): Whether an answer to an incompletely conditioned request is permitted is disputed: it is barred by the view requiring an answer when conditions are complete, but allowed by the other view. MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 (author): For a request aligned with welfare, the supplicant may either fulfill or fall short of the conditions for asking. JISHUMI, d. 494 (author): Supplication is worship when it fulfills its conditions. JISHUMI, d. 494 (author): When the conditions hold, God answers if answering benefits the petitioner and delays if delay is more beneficial; human welfare cannot depend on their choice and request. BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 (author): Supplication has manners and conditions that cause acceptance; those who fulfill them are eligible for an answer, while those who violate them transgress and do not deserve one. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The order places praise before supplication, as Abraham first praised God and then prayed; Razi compares this sequence with Abraham's words. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (بعض الجهال): They claim prayer resembles giving orders or prohibitions, which they regard as bad manners toward a generous, merciful Lord. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (قيل): Some say supplication must be free of grammatical solecism, as a poem says a lion who calls his Lord with solecism gets no answer. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The hadith's question expresses how unlikely acceptance is for someone in that condition; answering requires conditions in the supplicant, prayer, and requested thing. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Likely times and circumstances for answered supplication include pre-dawn, breaking the fast, between call and commencement of prayer, Wednesday afternoon, distress, travel, illness, rain, and battle ranks. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): Supplication should use transmitted wording, avoid contrived pre-Islamic rhyming prose, and be grammatically correct. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): He lists hoped-for times and places for answered prayer, including dawn, the last third of night, breaking the fast, between calls, distress, rain, battle, Eid, the Friday hour, the Kaʿba, the Prophet’s chamber, and al-Aqṣā. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (إبراهيم التيمي): A saying transmitted by Ibrahim al-Taymi holds that one who praises God before supplicating has secured a response, while one who supplicates first remains hopeful. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Supplication has conditions and courtesies that cause an answer; one who neglects them commits excess and does not merit a response. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Some deny that any prophet's grave is certainly located, apart from the Prophet's; Abraham's is said to be within the enclosure but not precisely identified, while prayers near righteous graves are reported as tested under known conditions. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Al-Fatiha had already been described as the Sura of Supplication and Teaching the Request, and as instruction in the etiquette of prayer. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Supplication and command are requests in the same grammatical form: a needy person’s cry for help is a prayer, while the helper’s “get up” is a response and command. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The greater’s aid to the distressed is a mark of greatness; obedience to the greater is also required by good manners, reason, and the subjects’ own benefit, and rational action is called rushd. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): God’s unrestricted power and necessary freedom remain intact: the limits described concern the particular act and its conditions, not the agent, just as human ability to give, see, and hear is expressed through organs. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): A particular act of creating Zayd depends on parents, time, place, conditions, and absence of obstacles; it is the effect, not the divine agent, that depends on these causes. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The reported etiquettes of prayer help bring a servant closer to the true reality of prayer and petition. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (الصادق عليه السلام): Asked why “Call Me and I will answer” seemed unfulfilled, al-Ṣādiq says to obey God and follow the proper form: praise and glorify Him, recall and thank His blessings, bless Muḥammad and his family, confess sins, and seek forgiveness. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): The author concludes that God will answer a servant who supplicates with proper etiquette. QIRAAT-ER (Y-iḍ): A fatḥa on the yāʾ is grammatically valid alongside bī and adds phonetic weight to the divine self-reference. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT (author): Though both genders are grammatically possible, the verse chooses masculine قريب; the author explains that an إضافة can take gender from its complement when it is part-like or nearly so. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): When events occur in accordance with a supplicant's aim, this indicates a world-governing agent who hears prayer; otherwise the desired result would not occur at that time. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (جابر بن عبد الله): Jabir says the Prophet prayed three times at the Conquest Mosque on Monday and Tuesday and was answered on Wednesday between prayers; Jabir sought that hour for grave troubles and recognized the answer. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (النبي عليه السلام): The Prophet instructs a supplicant to ask firmly for forgiveness rather than say 'if You will,' since no one can compel God. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (علماؤنا): Scholars say a supplicant should not qualify requests for forgiveness, mercy, or gifts with if You wish; he should ask decisively as someone in need. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Adding if You wish suggests indifference to God's mercy or gift, like asking someone whose help one does not need; the needy should be resolute. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Anas reports the Prophet's instruction to make one's request resolutely and not say grant it if You wish, since no one can compel God. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The Muwatta also quotes the wording, O God forgive me if You wish and have mercy on me if You wish."}, {"id": "2:186/q10/p2", "position": "Lawful food, obedience, and avoidance of sin or severing kinship matter.", "reasons": "THALABI, d. 427 (أبو سعيد): The Prophet says a Muslim's prayer without sin or severing kinship brings an immediate answer, an afterlife reserve, or protection from equivalent harm. JISHUMI, d. 494 (أبو علي): Abu Ali says the verse praises believers and implies that God answers believers' prayers rather than sinners; Abu Bakr al-Ikhshid allows answering an unbeliever's prayer as a gracious favor. BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 (عبادة بن الصامت): The Prophet says no Muslim prays without receiving what he asked or having equivalent harm averted, unless he asks for sin or severing kinship. BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 (أبو هريرة): The Prophet says God answers so long as a person does not pray for sin or severing kinship and does not become impatient; impatience is repeating the plea, seeing no answer, despairing, and abandoning prayer. TABRISI, d. 548 (النبي): Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports the Prophet saying that a Muslim's prayer without sin or severing kinship receives one of three outcomes: prompt fulfillment, a reward saved for the afterlife, or equivalent harm averted. The Companions ask if they should pray more, and he answers that God is more generous. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (author): Another answer is that supplication requires conditions rooted in obedience, including lawful food and a present heart; unlawful food blocks its answer. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أبو سعيد الخدري): Al-Qaffal transmits from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri a Prophetic report that a Muslim's prayer is answered by quick fulfillment, a store for the afterlife, or an equivalent evil averted, unless it asks for sin or severing kinship; Razi gives no grading. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (المعتزلة): The Muʿtazila restrict answered prayer to believers free of grave sin: being called answered is a great religious honor, incompatible with a sinner’s deserved disgrace; a sinner’s request may occur without counting as an answer. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): God says He does not love transgressors; al-Qurtubi counts anyone persisting in a major sin, knowingly or unknowingly, among them. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Unlawful food and its like also prevent a supplication from being answered. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that a Muslim who asks without sin or severing kin receives one of three outcomes; when asked if they should ask more, the Prophet replied that God is more generous. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Muslim's report from Abu Hurayra adds that prayer continues to be answered unless the supplicant asks for sin or severing kin, or becomes impatient and gives up. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Other conditions on the supplicant are avoiding unlawful food and not tiring of supplication. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The requested matter must be legally permissible to ask for and do; the cited report excludes sin and severing kinship, which includes Muslims' rights and wrongs. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (سهل بن عبد الله التستري): Sahl al-Tustari lists seven conditions: humility, fear, hope, persistence, reverence, generality, and lawful food. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (المعتزلة)

: The Muʿtazila restrict answered prayer as a praiseworthy description to believers who have not mixed faith with wrongdoing; a sinner may get what he asked for without that being called an answer. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أبو هريرة): Muslim reports that prayer continues to be answered unless it asks for sin or severing kinship, or the servant grows impatient; impatience is repeating that one prayed without seeing an answer, then tiring of prayer and abandoning it. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (عليه السلام): A report says a Muslim's prayer is not rejected except when it asks for sin or severing kinship; otherwise its good may be stored for the Hereafter or evil averted in proportion to the prayer. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Among the special conditions is purifying the supplicant, beginning with bodily purification through lawful food; a proverb calls lawful food the teeth of supplication's key to heaven. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (author): These outcomes apply when supplication stays within bounds; transgression in prayer is forbidden and 7:55 forbids it. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (علي): Ali tells Nawf that God instructed David to require pure hearts, humble eyes, and clean hands from worshippers, and said He would not answer anyone while they wronged another creature. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (اسماعيل بن همام عن أبي الحسن عليه السلام): A single private prayer by a servant equals seventy public prayers. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (سلمان وجابر وعبد الله بن عمر وأنس بن مالك وابن أبي مغيث): Al-Durr al-Manthūr cites eight Prophetic reports through several Companions, all of which mention raising hands in prayer."}, {"id": "2:186/q10/p3", "position": "Sincerity, exclusive reliance on God, and a heart aligned with the spoken request are essential.", "reasons": "TABRISI, d. 548 (النبي): Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the Prophet saying God may defer a beloved servant's request because He loves hearing the servant's voice, but quickly grant a sincere request from a servant He dislikes because He hates hearing that voice. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): If responding to God means assent of heart and tongue, it is faith, making “respond to Me and believe in Me” seem redundant. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (قيل): Another account gives four conditions: guarding the heart in solitude, tongue among people, eyes from the forbidden, and stomach from unlawful food. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The supplicant needs sincere intent and an attentive heart; God does not answer a heedless, distracted heart. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عطاء): Ibn Ata names the pillars as presence of heart, compassion, resignation, and humility; sincerity is its wings, pre-dawn its time, and blessings on Muhammad its cause. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): The command to believe is not a new conversion, since the passage addresses believers; it instead calls for lasting faith, sincerity, or belief in God’s promised answer. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (نافع بن معد يكرب): Ibn Mardawayh transmits an unusual report from Nāfiʿ ibn Maʿd Yakrib: he and ʿĀʾisha asked about the verse, and Gabriel conveyed God’s greeting and promise to answer the sincere servant’s call. Ibn Kathīr calls this route gharīb. BURHAN, d. 794 (أبو العباس): The written omission of the object pronoun in دعان signals a prayer arising from the unseen realm with inward sincerity. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): Every creature inwardly calls through need even without speech; the explicit clause requires spoken supplication to match the sincerity of that inward state. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (نافع بن معد يكرب): Nafiʿ ibn Maʿd Yakrib reports that ʿAʾisha asked the Prophet about the verse; Gabriel conveyed God’s greeting and promise to answer her sincere, pious prayer. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The sayings attributed to Gabriel and Abraham are, fitting their station, eloquent forms of prayer; silent state can speak more eloquently than words for a sincere person in God’s presence. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Asking and seeking help from God means relying on Him as the true source: ordinary causes have only the limited, God-given role of pathways and intermediaries, so exclusive reliance on them is misplaced. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): This teaching does not abolish created causes: a person asks with the heart, speaks with the tongue, and employs bodily organs, just as giving, seeing, and hearing require a hand, eye, and ear. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): These reports point to persistence: repeatedly pursuing a sincere intention purifies it. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Keeping prayer private protects the sincerity of the request. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The promise applies to a genuine caller whose innate knowledge and desire unite heart and tongue; prayer is what the heart bears and the tongue of natural disposition voices, not words used in jest or falsehood. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): A request made by natural disposition to God does not miss its answer; an apparently unanswered prayer must lack either genuine asking or exclusive reliance on God. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The prayer passages just cited contain prayer’s pillars and etiquette; their central requirement is sincerity, with heart and tongue aligned, detachment from every cause besides God, and reliance on Him. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The preceding reports call for sincerity in prayer; they do not deny created causes, which God appoints as intermediaries rather than independent sources of effect. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Innate desire can oppose a person's words or imagined wishes, like the sick child who rejects bitter medicine while naturally seeking health; the natural order is sound, whereas imagination often errs, so the reports concern the heart’s true request. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): ʿAlī’s phrase “the gift is according to intention” means the response matches what the heart truly intends, not necessarily the wording that the tongue displays. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Prayer is one form of worship; the closest, warmest relation with God is formed in prostration and in sincere supplication. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The supplicant must know that only God can meet the need and that all intermediaries are under His control. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): One who asks revenge for another’s wrongdoing accepts the same standard for every comparable case; if that petitioner has wronged someone, the request applies to him too, while unwillingness to accept that result shows the prayer is not genuine."}, {"id": "2:186/q10/p4", "position": "An attentive heart and sound knowledge of God are needed.", "reasons": "THALABI, d. 427 (إبراهيم بن أدهم): Ibrahim ibn Adham says prayers go unanswered because people know God and the Prophet without obeying or following the Sunna, neglect the Qur'an and gratitude, ignore the afterlife and death, and fixate on others' faults. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): A genuine petitioner must know God; otherwise he calls an imagined nonexistent object rather than God. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): God does not disappoint a supplicant or become distracted from the prayer; He hears supplication. The verse encourages prayer, which is never lost with Him. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عبد الله بن عمرو): ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr reports the Prophet’s analogy of hearts as vessels, some more receptive than others, and urges people to ask with certainty: God does not answer a servant who calls with a heedless heart. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (معاذ بن جبل عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Muʿadh reports the Prophet saying that with true knowledge of God, mountains would move in response to one’s supplication. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Loud prayer suits the heedless by driving away stray thoughts, while subdued prayer suits people present with God. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Those who belittle supplication also belittle worship, fail to know God as near and responsive, and instead value the attention of creatures or take them as rivals. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم): Mu'adh ibn Jabal transmits the Prophet's saying that true knowledge of God would make mountains move through one's supplication. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Heedlessness and distraction prevent the reality of prayer and petition from taking place. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (الصادق عليه السلام): Al-Ṣādiq says God does not answer a prayer made with an inattentive heart. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (علي عليه السلام): ʿAlī says God does not accept a prayer from a heedless heart. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): “Know God in ease and He will know you in hardship” means invoke Him while things are easy; one who forgets God then treats causes as independent and only acknowledges lordship conditionally in distress."}, {"id": "2:186/q10/p5", "position": "One must avoid impatience, despair, and abandoning prayer.", "reasons": "TUSTARI (author): Responding means supplicating and believing means affirming the present God without despair. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A sound report says prayer is answered so long as a person does not become impatient and complain that it has gone unanswered. e stated qualities may expect an answer, but others must not despair; the text cites the prohibition on despairing from God’s mercy. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (قائلون منهم): Some say abandoning sins itself functions as prayer, since God then takes charge of one’s affairs. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra reports that a servant continues to receive an answer so long as he is not impatient, saying, ‘I prayed, but my prayer was not answered.’ The report is in both Ṣaḥīḥs. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أنس): Anas reports the Prophet’s statement that a servant remains in a good state unless he becomes impatient, which means saying that he prayed but God did not answer. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عائشة): ʿĀʾisha says a believer’s prayer either comes quickly in this life or is stored for the next, unless the person is impatient or despairing; she defines both as saying they asked but received no answer. ʿUrwa narrates her explanation. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (سعيد بن المسيب): Ibn Qusayṭ says he heard Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib teach exactly what ʿĀʾisha taught about a prayer’s fulfillment, unless the supplicant is impatient or despairing. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (علي): Ali reports that after the Prophet urged people not to tire of prayer and cited 40:60, a man asked whether God hears supplication; this verse was revealed. SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 (علي): Ali reports that after the Prophet urged people not to tire of supplication, a man asked whether God hears prayer; the verse was then revealed. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): The threat of Hell for abandoning prayer concerns abandoning worship altogether, not merely one branch of worship; this shows that prayer is the root of worship. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Prayer with despair or hesitation shows that the person is not truly asking; the source also reports a prohibition on praying for what cannot be. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): A cited hadith says each person’s prayer is answered unless they grow impatient and complain that it was not answered."}, {"id": "2:186/q10/p6", "position": "A request for the impossible or harmful is not a true eligible prayer.", "reasons": "BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 (author): Other explanations limit the general wording: God answers if He wills, if the request accords with the decree, if the answer is good for the petitioner, or if the request is not impossible; the first is compared to 6:41. TABRISI, d. 548 (قيل): Another interpretation says God hears an invoker as a nearby person hears them; nearness of distance itself is impossible for God because it belongs to created beings situated in a place. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): If God occupied a place and were perceptible, He would be divisible; dependence on parts would make Him possible and originated, which is impossible for the eternal Creator. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): A spatial occupant must be infinite in all directions, infinite in only some, or finite throughout; the first two are impossible and the third is rejected by both sides, so God is not in a direction. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (بعض الجهال): They argue that all events must ultimately follow from the eternal necessary cause; what it eternally wills is inevitable and what it does not will is impossible, so prayer cannot affect fixed destinies. ITQAN, d. 911 (author): The general rule is that an attribute whose literal reality is impossible for God is interpreted through its necessary implication. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): The verse promises an answer to the supplicant, while apparent unanswered prayers are qualified by 6:41: by God's will, in accordance with decree, not for an impossible request, or when answering is good for the petitioner. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): God's nearness is metaphorical, since spatial proximity is impossible for Him; it denotes His knowledge of servants' acts and words and awareness of their states. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (Îcâb veya cebir nazariyelerine saplananlar): The objectors argue that a request already known by God to occur must occur necessarily, while one not known to occur is impossible, so prayer is needless either way. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The second fatalist objection says events are fixed by an eternal cause: what it decreed is necessary, what it did not decree impossible, so prayer can neither increase nor decrease destiny. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Knowing God means accepting that supplication can bring about customary impossibilities that are not intrinsically impossible; the main prophetic miracles are answered prayers. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): One failure is that the person has not truly asked: ignorance may lead someone to request what cannot happen or what they would not want if they knew its reality, as with asking for cure rather than a dead person's return to life. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (علي عليه السلام): ʿAlī corrects a man who sought refuge from “trial”: wealth and children themselves are called a trial in 64:15, so he should seek refuge from misleading trials instead."}]}
{"id": "2:186/q11", "question": "What role does supplication have beside decree and ordinary causes?", "turns_on": "The disagreement turns on whether prayer is a cause within decree or futile before fixed outcomes, and on whether surrender calls for silence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:186/q11/p1", "position": "Prayer is a real cause within God's decree, while God remains sovereign over effects.", "reasons": "THALABI, d. 427 (بعضهم): Some restrict the general promise: prayers are answered only if God wills, accord with decree, avoid impossibility, or are beneficial; Abu Sa'id's report says a sinless, non-severing prayer receives one of three outcomes. THALABI, d. 427 (إبراهيم بن أدهم): Ibrahim ibn Adham says prayers go unanswered because people know God and the Prophet without obeying or following the Sunna, neglect the Qur'an and gratitude, ignore the afterlife and death, and fixate on others' faults. BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 (author): Supplication has manners and conditions that cause acceptance; those who fulfill them are eligible for an answer, while those who violate them transgress and do not deserve one. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet prayed that his community would not fight among themselves, but that prayer was denied because destiny had decreed otherwise. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام): A saying attributed to the Prophet states that God decreed the measures before creating creation by a specified number of years; opponents cite it to argue that prayer cannot change destiny. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عطاء): Ibn Ata likens supplication to a structure with pillars, wings, causes, and times: when these fit, it gains strength, ascends, and succeeds. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): Prayer is a supreme act of servitude because it displays dependence on God; revelation and the prophets command and practice it, refuting those who say it has no benefit. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (قائلون ممن يسمون علماء الحقيقة): One group says prayer is appropriate for afterlife matters but unnecessary for worldly needs because God already undertakes them. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Supplication has conditions and courtesies that cause an answer; one who neglects them commits excess and does not merit a response. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The prophetic answer preserves a middle position: neither absolute compulsion nor unrestricted freedom, but a balance of divine determination and human choice, with people facilitated rather than coerced. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The predestination objection is incomplete: some outcomes are decreed conditional on supplication, just as satiety depends on eating and success on seeking and effort. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Created beings, not God, are subject to decree; prayer acknowledges divine precedence and is therefore a high form of worship. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Since events are tied to causes and effort follows laws, supplication is itself one of the causes through which decreed outcomes occur. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The second fatalist objection says events are fixed by an eternal cause: what it decreed is necessary, what it did not decree impossible, so prayer can neither increase nor decrease destiny. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The verse rebukes people who shout and make a commotion in prayer because they imagine God is difficult to hear or far away. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (اليهود وغيرهم): An objection says the requested need is either already decreed, and therefore necessary, or not decreed, and therefore impossible; either way prayer cannot affect it. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Predetermination does not make a thing independent of its causes; prayer itself is one cause, so when it occurs its effect can occur.
